svg.title: Conceptual distinction between current scFMs and VCFM objectives
svg.desc: A paper-style page showing a table that compares typical scFM emphasis with stricter VCFM requirements.

g.text: Table 1: Conceptual distinction between current scFMs and the stricter VCFM objective.
Why VCFMs Require Stricter Evaluation Than Current scFMs

text.tspan: Most current scFM benchmarks prioritize tasks such as cell type annotation, batch correction,
clustering, retrieval, imputation, and masked reconstruction. These tasks are useful for evaluating
representation quality, but they only partially probe whether a model captures the functional
organization of cellular systems. A model can succeed on them by learning smooth correlational
This limitation becomes especially important when models are described as virtual cells. The
term suggests that the model can support in silico experimentation. Yet a cell embedding bench-
mark tells us little about whether the model can predict the direction, magnitude, or heterogeneity
of response under targeted perturbation. Similarly, strong integration performance does not imply
correct temporal ordering, causal structure, or plausible cross-modal coupling.
A VCFM, explicitly or implicitly, makes a stronger claim than “I encode cells well.” It suggests that
the model can be used to reason about latent mechanisms, anticipate novel responses, and generate
realistic state trajectories. These claims are closer to surrogate experimentation than to generic
feature extraction. As a result, evaluation must move from surface-level predictive convenience
toward deeper tests of model validity.
This stricter standard is not a matter of rhetorical purity; it is a matter of scientific risk. If
a model is used to prioritize perturbations, nominate targets, infer regulatory control points, or
simulate unseen conditions, then errors are qualitatively different from ordinary classification mis-
takes. The cost of biologically implausible predictions can be high, especially when such predictions
